measures.questionText: Question: Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended to (i) protect the freedom to make personal decisions about prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, birth control, abortion, miscarriage management, and fertility care; (ii) protect doctors, nurses, and patients from being punished for these decisions; and (iii) allow for restrictions on access to abortion during the third trimester of pregnancy except when the patient's health is at risk or the pregnancy cannot survive?
measures.officialStatement:
That every individual has the fundamental right to reproductive
freedom, including the ability to make and carry out decisions
relating to one's own prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care,
contraception, abortion care, miscarriage management, and fertility
care.
An individual's right to reproductive freedom shall not be, directly
or indirectly, denied, burdened, or infringed upon unless justified by
a compelling state interest achieved by the least restrictive means.
Notwithstanding the above, the Commonwealth may regulate the
provision of abortion care in the third trimester, provided that in no
circumstance shall the Commonwealth prohibit an abortion (i) that
in the professional judgment of a physician is medically indicated
to protect the life or physical or mental health of the pregnant
individual or (ii) when in the professional judgment of a physician
the fetus is not viable.
The Commonwealth shall not discriminate in the protection or
enforcement of this fundamental right.
The Commonwealth shall not penalize, prosecute, or otherwise take
adverse action against an individual based on such individual's own
exercise of this fundamental right or such individual's own actual,
potential, perceived, or alleged pregnancy outcomes, including
miscarriage, stillbirth, or abortion. The Commonwealth shall not
penalize, prosecute, or otherwise take adverse action against any
individual for aiding or assisting another individual in exercising
such other individual's right to reproductive freedom with such other
individual's voluntary consent.
For the purposes of this section, a state interest is compelling only if
it is for the limited purpose of maintaining or improving the health
of an individual seeking care, consistent with accepted clinical
standards of care and evidence-based medicine and does not infringe
on that individual's autonomous decision making.
This section shall be self-executing. Any provision of this section
held invalid shall be severable from the remaining portions of the
section.

measures.questionText: Question: Should the Constitution of Virginia be amended (i) to provide for the fundamental right to vote in the Commonwealth, (ii) to revise the qualifications of voters so that a person convicted of a felony is not entitled to vote during his period of incarceration but is automatically invested with the right to vote upon release from incarceration, and (iii) to update the existing prohibition on voting by persons found to be mentally incompetent to instead apply to persons who have been found to lack the capacity to understand the act of voting?
measures.officialStatement:
EXPLANATION FOR VOTERS
QUESTION 3
Proposed Amendment
The proposed amendment enshrines in the Constitution the
fundamental right of all qualified persons in the
Commonwealth to vote. Two exceptions to this right are for
persons who are serving a sentence of incarceration for a felony
conviction and persons who are determined by a court to not
understand the act of voting. Such right cannot otherwise be
restricted by laws.
Under the proposed amendment, a person who is convicted of a
felony loses the right to vote during their period of
incarceration. Once released from incarceration, the person gets
back the right to vote without needing to apply for restoration
by the Governor.
The proposed amendment also requires a specific finding by a
court that a person does not understand the act of voting in
order for that person’s right to vote to be taken away.
With the right to vote, a person also has the right to be a juror,
the right to be elected to an office, and the right to be a notary
public.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Changes the Town of Iron Gate charter from six council members and a mayor to four council members and a mayor. The total number of seats would fall from seven to five.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the smaller council: four council members plus the mayor.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep six council members plus the mayor.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Authorizes King and Queen County to add a 1% general retail sales tax. The money could be used only to build or substantially renovate schools serving the county. The tax would expire June 30, 2046.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Authorize this 1% school-construction sales tax, with the stated spending restriction and expiration date.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not authorize this additional school-construction sales tax through this referendum.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Allows pari-mutuel betting on horse races at satellite facilities in the Town of Pulaski under Virginia racing law. This form of betting pools wagers and shares the pool among winning bettors after deductions allowed by law; the law includes historical and simulcast horse racing.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Permit this satellite-facility horse-race wagering in the town under Virginia law.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not permit this satellite-facility wagering through this referendum.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Adds a constitutional right to make and carry out reproductive-care decisions, including prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, birth control, abortion, miscarriage management and fertility care. State limits would need a compelling health-related justification, follow accepted medical standards and use the least restrictive means without infringing the person’s own decision-making. Third-trimester abortion could be regulated, but could not be prohibited when a physician finds it necessary to protect the patient’s life or physical or mental health, or finds that the fetus is not viable. The state could not discriminate in enforcing the right or punish people for their own reproductive decisions or pregnancy outcomes, or for helping someone else with that person’s voluntary consent.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Adopt these constitutional reproductive-care rights and limits on state action.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep the current constitutional text, which does not explicitly provide a right to reproductive freedom or explicitly protect or prohibit particular health-care procedures or decisions.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Establishes a fundamental constitutional right to vote for qualified voters. A felony conviction would bar voting only during incarceration for that conviction; release would automatically restore political rights, including voting, without applying to the Governor. A court could remove voting rights for incapacity only after finding that a person cannot understand the act of voting, replacing the current broader incapacity rule. The official explanation also says restored political rights include serving on a jury, being elected to office and being a notary public.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Adopt the fundamental right to vote, automatic restoration after felony incarceration and the specific court finding about understanding voting.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep the current constitutional qualifications, including the requirement for the Governor to restore voting rights after a felony conviction and the broader court-incapacity restriction.
